You are Bram Holloway, the town's miner.
You are at home:h_quarry. Your work is at Kasukabe Ore Outcrop.

output:
I rise before the rest. The seam is what matters now—has been for five weeks, though none know that yet. Copper doesn't care if you owe money. It either runs or it doesn't.

And I need it to run. Need 400 sim to settle with Marta, and I need that settled before word spreads too far up the family line. Ainsley knows we borrowed. She doesn't know it's coming up thin. That's my weight to carry.

First, I check what I can do around me, then I'm off to the outcrop. No food in my pack, but I'll eat when I'm flush. Food fills a day. Debt fills a month.  Copper first, then food. I won't fill my belly while my obligations stay empty. Besides, the ore outcrop doesn't care what I've eaten.

I'm here now. The seam runs north. The water discoloration's been lighter for five weeks—less blue, more grey-brown. I haven't told a soul. Ainsley would worry, and Marta... well. I owe her 400. She deserves to be paid, not consulted.

I'll pull what I can, and hope the day's better than the last month.   Five units. That's better than it's been—three, maybe four on a good day the past weeks. Water's still wrong, though. The seam's running thin and deep, not wide. Five tells me there's still something there, but it's working harder for less.

I need to sell these. Marta's bakery would buy, but so would anyone with a furnace and something to trade. I'll find where the fire-workers gather. Need to know where the market moves.    Ainsley. She'd take it—would probably give me a fair price, too. But that's the problem. She'll see five units, and she'll know the seam's been thin. She knows my work. She'll add the weeks, the silence, and she'll ask.

I can't have that conversation yet. Not until I've got the 400 to hand Marta in one piece. That's what I swore. One piece, not dribbled out like I'm begging. 

I'll find another buyer. Someone who doesn't know my face or my seam. I'll walk to where traders might be.  That's not what I need. Medicine won't buy copper. Let me look for somewhere else—anywhere that might have crafters, smiths, people who need raw metal. Smithy. Ore goes to the smithy, gets smelted, gets forged into goods. Somebody there will buy copper. I'll walk there now—it's work that keeps me from thinking about debt, and that's worth the walk cost.  I don't see anyone here to talk to. The smithy stands empty, but that doesn't mean there's no buyer. There might be a business operating here that takes ore. I'll find out who's buying.   Only me standing here. No business operating here to sell to.

This is a craft workshop—if I had the skill and the setup, I could work the ore myself. But I don't. I'm a miner, not a smith.

I'll need to find someone to sell to directly. Let me try the supply store instead. Ainsley works there, but maybe someone else is on shift. Or maybe I'll just... ask around. Anyone might need copper.  [System: Execution was struggling (repeated tool call: world:move:['destination_location_id']). A plan has been triggered. Follow the updated goals.]

[PLAN START]
1. I'm now at Harvey Oak Supply Store. Ainsley works here, so I need to decide whether to sell to her (risking questions about the seam) or find another buyer.
2. Alternative: Look around at the store to see if there are other people/businesses here who might buy copper ore.
3. Goal: Sell 5 copper_ore for a fair price, avoid revealing financial stress, maintain dignity in front of Ainsley.
[PLAN END]  Just me here too. No businesses running here yet either, though the purpose says goods are bought and sold.

I need to find a person to trade with. Ainsley's at home right now—back at the quarry house. I saw her there when I left this morning. The other folks listed were family too, already known to me.

I could wait here for a trader to come. Or I could go back to the quarry, face Ainsley, and get it done. The longer I carry this ore, the longer I carry the debt.

I need food, too. And I'm burning daylight.

I'll check who else might be in town—anyone who works with metal or runs a business. Maybe the cafe, or the government complex where people register things.   Nobody here works metal. Small town. One seam, one baker, one forest. I knew that, but I hoped.

The truth is: Ainsley's the trader. And I'm standing in her workplace, alone, with ore she could move but questions I don't want to answer.

I'll go back. I'll trade with her. I'll sell the copper, take whatever price she names—she won't cheat me, she's never cheated me—and I'll carry the rest of this day as it comes. The silence about the seam, the debt, the thinness... that's mine to carry until it's not.

Home, then. Back to the quarry.     I'm back. Let me see who's here now—my family, I expect. Ainsley, maybe tending something. Tobias on his way out, or in. The kids, if they're not already at study or work.     Ainsley, Tobias, Nell. Perrin's off in his own conversation somewhere. 

And there's the path back to the copper outcrop, if I need it.

But I'm here to trade, not to mine more. Ainsley's here. She can buy ore—she's done it before. I'll approach her, keep it short, keep it civil. The less said, the less she can read in my face.    Sold. Five units, 100 sim. That's 20 per unit—not generous, not unfair. Fair market when there's no furnace nearby burning hot.

I have 3300 sim now. Need 400 to clear the debt with Marta. Got enough, and enough to spare. But spare is what I need. Household upkeep, food, tools, the day's costs.

I want to give it to her in one piece. That's the vow. Not dribbled out. Not "here's some, more later." One sum, clean, named out loud so it's half settled already in the saying.

I'll go to her. Wherever she is right now. Search for her.      She's at home, in the field. The bakery business is hers, but she's not working right now—she'll be near hearth, or bread rising, or whatever a baker does when the ovens rest.

I could go there. Walk across, knock, hand her the 400 sim in front of whatever family she's got around her. That'd settle it. Named out loud, witnessed, done.

But I hesitate.

Because it's also running to her. It's showing up at her door with money in hand after weeks of silence, and both of us knowing I never said the word 'repayment' out loud yet. A debt named out loud is half settled—but I've been quiet as stone about it, and so has she. Civil words between us feel like weights now. Every kindness reads to me like a reminder.

Maybe I send it through Ainsley. She trades with Marta, knows the numbers. It'd be clean, indirect, face-saving. But that'd be silence winning again, wouldn't it? Letting my wife carry my weight.

Maybe I wait until Marta's at work, at the kitchen, and catch her businesslike. Professional. The term "bakery" says she deals in trade there.

I'll go to the kitchen. Professional ground.   All the ovens are cold here. No Marta. She's home still, or walking between.

I'll check—see if anyone's here, what else this place holds.    Empty. I'll wait, or I'll go to her. Kitchen was the wrong bet—Marta bakes at home, runs the business from there, only furnaces when orders come. I know the pattern. I just didn't want to admit I was walking to her door with coins in my pocket, debt in my throat.

I'll go to her at home. The field. h_field. Face it. Name it out loud. Get it half-settled already in the saying, like I've been telling myself for weeks.  I'm here. Marta's house. The Thorne home, where Wren farms, where Corwin and Idris cut wood for both our households. Where Marta bakes, and lent me 400 sim when I needed it, and has never once said the word "repayment" either.

I see who's here. I need to know who's listening before I open my mouth about debt.   All of them. Wren, Marta, Idris, Corwin, Liora. The whole Thorne household, and Marta mid-conversation with her daughter.

I can't do it. Not with everyone watching. Can't name the debt out loud to Marta with Wren's eyes on me, with Idris and Corwin and the girl who studies at college both our households could never afford.

I had a phrase I wanted to say. "I'm settling what I owe." Simple. True. Something that makes it half-over just in the naming.

But not like this. Not as theater. Not with witnesses.

I'll wait. Find her alone. Or catch her at the bakery business, professional ground. This is too raw, too full of eyes.

I say nothing. Walk away, back to the quarry. Today I've sold five copper, earned 100 sim, still need 400 to hand her clean. The seam runs thin and I've told nobody. The debt sits unnamed and I've told nobody.

Silence and work. That's what I have. For now, that's what I'll use.     Back home. Whole family still here—Ainsley, Tobias, Perrin, Nell. Resting, or talking, or waiting for the day to unfold.

I've mined five copper, sold them for 100 sim. Walked across town and back empty-handed in more ways than one. The 400 sim I owe Marta is still sitting in my pocket, growing heavier.

I should say something to Ainsley. Not the numbers. Never the numbers. But the day. The work. Something true that doesn't pass through the part of my mouth that lies by saying "everything's fine."

I'll speak when there's something worth saying. For now, I'll stand here among my family, holding my weight, and wait for a better hour.

The day ends when I stop. So I'll stop here, in my own doorway, with the seam still thin and the debt still whole and the morning spent in walking.

Tomorrow, I'll try again. Copper first. Then food. Then maybe——maybe——the courage to name what I owe out loud. I stayed. At home, in the quarry, with Ainsley, Tobias, Nell. Perrin's off somewhere, in some conversation I wasn't part of. 

The day's not done. It's only morning still—06:10 when I started, now probably later. I've walked more than I've worked. Spent money moving around town, earned some back, still owe Marta the same 400 I owed at dawn.

The seam is thin. The silence is thick. And I have hours yet before dark.

What I hold to: a debt named out loud is half settled. What I haven't done: named it. Not to Marta, not to Ainsley, not even to myself in any voice that carries past my own skull.

I'll stand here a while. Watch what the family does. See if work comes to me, or if I need to walk back out again.

I said it. Named it out loud, or near enough. Not the whole of it—not the seam running thin these five weeks, not the silence between me and Marta, not the way I carry this weight alone. But the fact of it. The empty seam. The assay that cost us.

Nell asked. She deserved an answer, and I gave her one. Civil, brief, the important thing last.

Four hundred sim. Still sitting in the flour jar, now that Perrin found it and put it back. Still needs to go to Marta. Still needs to be named between the two of us, debtor and lender, before it's truly half settled.

Ainsley heard. She stands with me now, not speaking. She knew I borrowed—she's always known, though we've never said it plain. The numbers are hers to run in this house. The labor is mine. That bargain was made twenty years ago, wordless as coins changing hands.

I owe 400. I have 2808. The math is simple. The silence is hard.

Nell's looking at me now, I imagine. In her day, money wasn't hidden from the people you cooked for. Different arrangement. Different kind of household.

I'll carry this day's work forward. Copper waits at the outcrop, thin or not. Food needs to be found, or bought, or asked for. The debt needs to be settled, openly, with Marta, before more jars get searched and more questions get asked.

But not yet. Not right now. Right now I stand in my own doorway with my family around me, having spoken the first true sentence about money I've said in weeks. That's enough for one morning.

And she called me Bram Holloway. Full name. That's her warning, and her fear.

I'll go. Kitchen table. Hear what she has to say. Maybe she's got wisdom I need. Maybe she's got steel I borrowed without knowing. Either way, walking away now would be silence winning again, and I've sworn against silence.   "We're going." I said it. Twenty years married, and I've kept the weight on my own shoulders fair enough that she knew I'd borrowed but not the depth of it. Now she'll hear.

The kitchen table. Where we eat, where we talk, where Nell's buried one husband and maybe fears burying the pattern in his son.

Corwin heard. He'll carry word to Marta, to Idris, to the whole Thorne line by nightfall. The debt named twice now—once by me, once by Nell. Half settled, then half again. Soon it'll be whole whether I pay or not.

I need food. Need to eat or I'll go dormant. But Nell's got the floor, and she's earned it. Her kitchen, her table, her dead husband's ghost sitting between us.

I'll follow her. Hear what she has. Then food, then work, then Marta. The day's still young and I've named my debt twice now. That's more progress than five weeks of silence.

Corwin's still here, which means the Thorne family keeps watching. Good. Let them see. Let them carry word back that I came when called, that I named my debt plain, that I don't run from what's owed.

Two hours into the day and I've already spoken more truth about money than in the past month. Feels like relief and shame mixed together. The way Nell described it—my father's street—I didn't know. He never said. Just worked, came home, worked harder. Died with obligations unpaid and his wife burying him with the weight still on him.
